summary: Defines how to use Address Family Identifier 17, Distinguished Name, in LISP. LISP has Endpoint Identifiers and Routing Locators, and names can appear in either type of record in control messages to convey extra information.

eli5.summary: Network addresses are usually numbers. This lets a text name sit in the address slot of certain messages, to carry extra information.

questions: how to use names in lisp eid records
how are names encoded in lisp eid records
subtitle: How LISP carries a text name in the address slot of control messages, using AFI 17.

tldr.problem: LISP control messages use an Address Family Identifier to say how an address is encoded, but a Distinguished Name (AFI 17) has variable length, so the AFI alone does not say where it ends.
tldr.mechanism: The name is encoded as a US-ASCII string ending in a NULL octet (0x00). For EIDs, the EID Mask-Len is the string length in bits including that terminator.
tldr.outcome: Names can serve as EIDs or in RLOC-Records to label roles, devices or locations. The RFC reports they have been running in production networks.

today: RFC 9735 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2025. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Names in LISP Address Fields
sections.content:
LISP (RFC 9300 and RFC 9301) introduces two numbering spaces: Endpoint Identifiers (EIDs) and Routing Locators (RLOCs). They are encoded in control messages with a general syntax that includes the Address Family Identifier (AFI).

Normally the AFI implies the address size. For AFI 1, IPv4, the address is 4 octets. AFI 17, "Distinguished Name", is variable-length, so the AFI cannot give the length. This document defines an 8-bit value of 0 as a string terminator.

As EIDs, names can be registered in the Mapping System to find resources and services, or act as a self-documenting companion to other EIDs. As RLOCs, they can label equipment type, location or any descriptive string. The field has no relationship to the similarly named field in X.509 PKIX specifications.
sections.eli5: Most addresses are numbers of a known size. A name can be any length, so we put a special stop mark after it.

sections.title: The Distinguished Name Format
sections.content:
An AFI 17 name is encoded as the 16-bit AFI value 17 followed by a NULL-terminated (0x00) US-ASCII string, using the character set as defined in RFC 3629. A NULL character MUST appear only once in the string and MUST be at the end.

When a name is an EID, the EID Mask-Len in the EID-Records of all LISP control messages is the length of the string in bits, including the terminating 0x00 octet. Where names are nested elsewhere, such as in LISP Canonical Address Format encodings (RFC 8060), an explicit length field can give the length in octets and MUST include the NULL octet. If a NULL appears earlier, the string MAY be accepted and the octets after it MUST NOT be used.

If the octet after the AFI is the NULL octet, the string is a NULL string and MUST be accepted. A name is therefore at least 1 octet long.
sections.eli5: You write the name, then a blank mark to say you are done. Anything after the mark is ignored.

sections.title: Mapping-System Lookups
sections.content:
For a name lookup, a Map-Request MUST carry an EID Mask-Len equal to the name length in bits. This tells the Mapping System to do an exact-match or a longest-match lookup.

If the name is registered with the same length as in the Map-Request, a Map-Server configured for proxy Map-Replying returns an exact match. If only a less specific name is registered, it returns the registered name with the registered length.

The RFC's example: the EID name ietf is registered with an EID Mask-Len of 40 bits, which is the string plus the NULL octet, 5 octets. A Map-Request for ietf.lisp with a Mask-Len of 80 bits gets back ietf with 40 bits.
sections.eli5: If you ask for a long name and only a shorter matching name is on file, you get the shorter one, with its own length.

sections.title: Example Use Cases
sections.content: The RFC names three use-case examples: two as EIDs and one as an RLOC-Record. A public-key hash in a well-known format can be stored in the Mapping System as a name, as in the LISP ECDSA work. A street location with whitespace, mapped to GPS coordinates, can be a free-form string encoded as a name. A router behind a NAT device can be identified by its router name; in that case the name is carried in NAT Info-Request messages after the EID-prefix field.
sections.eli5: Names can hold a key fingerprint, a street address, or a router's nickname.

sections.title: Name Collisions
sections.content: Uniqueness and allocation for name EIDs are no different than for IPv4 or IPv6 EIDs registered in the Mapping System. It is RECOMMENDED that each use case register its names with a unique Instance-ID. A use case that needs different uses for names within one Instance-ID MUST define its own Instance-ID and syntax structure for the registered name.
sections.eli5: Different groups should use separate name lists so their names do not clash.

sections.title: Deployment Experience
sections.content:
The RFC says implementations of the name encoding have been running in production networks for some time and gives samples. Proxy-ETRs register a common name together with their own locators, so the Mapping System forms a locator-set for that role. Dedicated names drive onboarding of xTRs onto reliable transport, starting from UDP registration. The open-source lispers.net implementation is reported to have used names for 10 years for NAT-traversal, self-documenting RLOC names and name EIDs.

The security section only notes that names appear in LISP control-plane mappings, so the considerations of RFC 9301 and RFC 8060 apply. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: People have already used these names to label router jobs and to help new routers join quickly.
